message:
feat(update): an HTTPS client for the update path, with the rules where they can be tested

The existing HTTP client cannot do this job -- POST only, responses truncated
at 64 KB, https refused outright -- and reworking something the whole product
depends on because the updater needs a GET would be the wrong trade. So the
updater gets its own client, and the directory client is left alone.

The two rules worth being certain about are that http:// is never accepted and
that a redirect is never followed down to cleartext. Both live in ordinary
functions with no I/O, because a rule buried in a WinHTTP callback can only be
checked by standing up a certificate authority, while a rule in a function can
be checked by calling it.

What this never does, in any configuration: set WINHTTP_OPTION_SECURITY_FLAGS,
continue past a certificate error, or follow https to http. TLS 1.2 at minimum
-- an update artifact runs with administrator rights and there is nothing to
negotiate down for. URLs carrying credentials are refused rather than parsed,
since reading as one host and resolving as another is the oldest trick there is.

Size limits abort rather than truncate. A truncated manifest would fail its
signature check anyway; stopping here leaves a reason instead of a puzzle. A
failed artifact download deletes its partial file so nothing later mistakes it
for a finished one.

One case opens a socket, and it is the one worth it: a loopback listener that
speaks plain HTTP, addressed as https://. The client has to fail, and the empty
body confirms it did not quietly speak cleartext instead. Nothing is disabled
to make that pass -- if a bypass is ever added, this case starts passing for
the wrong reason.

Not verified: a real round trip against a real HTTPS server. Doing that here
would mean trusting a certificate this test generated, and weakening validation
to prove validation works is not a trade worth making.

qwinsta: console active, rdp-tcp listening. 36 checks. Nothing was fetched from
the real directory server or the NAS.
